newsitem.title: USA: Dollar hit hard by remarks from former Treasury chief.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hit hard by remarks from former Treasury chief.

text.p: The dollar fell against most leading currencies Friday after former Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen said a stronger dollar could harm U.S. exporters.
Bentsen, in an interview with Reuters Financial Television, said he was "comfortable" with the dollar's current strong exchange rate.
But Bentsen, who helped push the dollar to record lows in 1995 by calling for a weak dollar, warned that any further gains by the dollar vs. the Japanese yen could reduce U.S. exports to Japan.
"If (the dollar) continues to rise and goes substantially above this, of course, it puts us at a competitive disadvantage. I would prefer not to see it increase in value," Bentsen said.

After briefly trading below the important 113 yen threshold, the dollar recovered somewhat when Robert Rubin, the current Treasury chief, told reporters at a press conference "we believe in a strong dollar."

"Bentsen's comment pushed it lower but then Treasury Secretary Rubin made a comment which took the dollar back up," said Kisoo Park, senior foreign exchange dealer at Bank of Boston. "I would presume Rubin carries more weight."
The dollar ended at 113.35 yen on Friday, down from 114.03 yen late Thursday.
Bentsen ran the Treasury department for the first two years of the Clinton Administration.
During Bentsen's tenure at the Treasury, many currency traders believed he favoured a semi-official cap on the dollar near 113 yen.

Bentsen at that time hinted he subscribed to a policy of benign neglect of the dollar, wherby a weaker U.S. currency would make U.S. exports to Japan more affordable and reduce the persistent trade gap between the two nations.
Largely as a result, the dollar hit a post-World War II low of 79.75 on April 19, 1995.
While traders said Bentsen's remarks may have only fleeting impact on the market, they echoed a recent chorus of complaints about the dollar's strength.

"The only thing it does signal is that there is still a body of opinion in the United States that does think the dollar is too strong at the moment," said Chris Iggo, an international economist at BZW/Barclays Bank in New York.
Many large U.S. coroporations, particularly the Big Three automakers, have recently complained the strong dollar is hurting their foreign sales.

The dollar had risen in early trading against the German mark and posted a 20-month high against the Swiss franc after a report showed U.S. wage inflation was flat in October, temporarily lifting U.S. bond prices.
"The dollar got a slight boost from the bonds, but I don't think the bonds turning (lower) made the dollar go down," said Mark Remigio, a vice president at Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi.

The dollar failed to hold its gains vs. the mark, which firmed in Asian trade after Ernst Welteke, a council member at the German central bank, or Bundesbank, told a Singapore audience he saw no need to cut German interest rates.
The dollar fell to 1.5143 marks, from 1.5180 marks on Thursday but rose to 1.2695 Swiss francs from 1.2680 Swiss.
It fell to Canadian $1.3340 from C$1.3385. The British pound touched its highest level since March 1995, closing at $1.6360, up from $1.6270.
